items.title: Anthropic files confidentially for IPO at $965B mark, $65B+ run rate
items.idea: Anthropic's Q2 revenue surged more than 14x YoY to a $65B+ run rate, and the company has filed confidentially with the SEC ahead of an expected fall debut. It was last privately valued around $965B after its May round — the first time it eclipsed OpenAI — with trial-balloon chatter now floating valuations near $2 trillion. Dario Amodei and co-founders are locking in supervoting shares, the same founder-control structure Zuckerberg (Meta) and Spiegel (Snap) used pre-IPO. Reportedly shopping too: in talks to buy Decart for ~$6B.
items.angle: This is the market's first real read on frontier-AI economics as a public asset — and the governance structure being copied from Meta/Snap tells you founders expect to keep control long after the roadshow ends.
items.tweetA: Anthropic's Q2 revenue grew 14x YoY to a $65B+ run rate. McDonald's took 68 years to reach $25B in revenue. Anthropic is filing to go public before its 5th birthday, at a $965B private mark. The comp set for 'growth company' just got rewritten.
items.tweetB: Dario Amodei is locking in Zuckerberg/Spiegel-style supervoting shares ahead of Anthropic's IPO. Founders keep the steering wheel, public shareholders get the growth story. Watch that governance template become the norm for every frontier-lab IPO this cycle.

charts.desc: No chart images in this email — roundup links out to source coverage of the IPO filing, valuation reporting, and governance structure.

items.title: Stripe pays $7.5B for OpenRouter — 5.8x its May mark, in 3 months
items.idea: Stripe's largest acquisition to date is the reported $7.5B purchase of OpenRouter, a 3-year-old AI model gateway that routes developer requests across 400+ models from 80+ providers. OpenRouter raised just $164M total and was marked at $1.3B as recently as May 2026. It serves the same developers pushing close to $2 trillion in payments through Stripe's infrastructure — OpenAI and Anthropic included.
items.angle: Stripe isn't buying model routing, it's buying the metering layer on AI token spend — managing tokens in and out is the same motion as managing cash in and out. That's a platform-of-platforms bet on tokens becoming the next unit of commerce.
items.tweetA: OpenRouter went from a $1.3B mark in May to a $7.5B Stripe acquisition in August — a 5.8x markup in three months on a company that's raised just $164M total. That's not an AI-bubble anecdote. That's the bubble's clearing price.
items.tweetB: Stripe didn't buy OpenRouter for the routing tech. It bought the toll booth on AI token spend — metering tokens in and out is the same motion as metering cash in and out. If tokens are the new unit of commerce, whoever owns that meter wins regardless of which model wins.

charts.desc: No charts in the roundup email; source article breaks down OpenRouter's funding history and the payments-infrastructure framing.

items.title: OpenAI's CFO: enterprise is now bigger than the ChatGPT consumer business
items.idea: OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told investors enterprise revenue has overtaken consumer — a deliberate repositioning ahead of its own confidential IPO filing, expected to follow Anthropic's float. Run rate is past $40B, roughly doubled since year-end. Underneath: a new CRO in under a year, senior sales leadership churn, aggressive Coding-product price moves to close the gap with Anthropic, and $500B of Ohio data-center fine print worth reading closely.
items.angle: Both frontier labs are now pitching 'enterprise SaaS company,' not 'consumer chatbot' — that's the framing the market will price at IPO, and it converges almost exactly with Anthropic's own enterprise-first story.
items.tweetA: OpenAI just told IPO investors enterprise revenue is now bigger than the ChatGPT consumer business everyone associates with the brand. Run rate past $40B, roughly doubled since January. The pitch has quietly flipped from 'AI for everyone' to 'AI for the enterprise.'
items.tweetB: New CRO in under a year at OpenAI, right as it preps a mega-IPO. Sales-leadership churn that close to a roadshow usually reads as a red flag — except revenue is doubling anyway. Worth checking whether that churn shows up as a risk factor in the S-1.

charts.desc: Charts inside — worth opening for the run-rate trajectory and the $500B Ohio data center deal breakdown.

items.title: Qwen passes Llama as the world's most-downloaded open AI model family
items.idea: Hugging Face's global open-source AI census shows Alibaba's Qwen family crossed 3 billion downloads, passing Meta's Llama and Google's open models as the most downloaded in the world. China's open-weight labs are shipping models nipping at the closed frontier at a fraction of the price — DeepSeek's new multimodal test model chasing Anthropic's Opus 4.8 was Friday's example — out of an academic-founder ecosystem executing 'way harder than it looks' under export-control conditions.
items.angle: Export controls were supposed to keep China behind on frontier AI. Instead they're producing the world's default open-weight distribution layer — a compute-demand signal for whichever domestic chips end up running those models at scale.
items.tweetA: Qwen just passed Llama and Google's open models to become the most-downloaded AI model family on Earth — 3 billion downloads. The open-source AI distribution layer's center of gravity has quietly moved to China while everyone was watching the closed-frontier race.
items.tweetB: Chip export controls were supposed to slow Chinese AI down. Instead DeepSeek's new model is reportedly chasing Anthropic's Opus 4.8, and Qwen leads global open-weight downloads. Sanctions didn't stop the models — they made China's labs the default distribution layer.

charts.desc: Charts inside — the Hugging Face report itself is chart-heavy on download share by country/lab.

items.title: AI industry's $3+ trillion in AI capex is sitting off the reported books
items.idea: SPVs, leases, and financing vehicles are putting Big Tech's true AI buildout trillions above the headline capex lines investors trade off of — a $3+ trillion gap between reported and actual spend, per this week's roundup of financing-structure reporting.
items.angle: If the capex numbers everyone models off of understate real spend by trillions, every depreciation-cliff and capex-intensity debate on the Street is running off the wrong base number.
items.tweetA: The AI capex debate everyone's having is about the wrong number. $3T+ of the actual buildout sits in SPVs and lease vehicles, off the reported capex lines analysts model from. The real depreciation cliff is bigger than the one Wall Street is bracing for.
items.tweetB: Off-balance-sheet financing for data centers is starting to rhyme with 2007 CDO structuring for mortgages. Nobody's asking who holds the residual risk in those SPVs if AI revenue growth disappoints. That's the tail risk nobody's pricing yet.

charts.desc: Charts inside — source piece breaks down SPV/lease structures by hyperscaler.

items.title: Jackson Hole: Warsh's topic is a decoy — the FX vol comes after the keynote
items.idea: Warsh speaks at Jackson Hole Friday 10:00am EDT on financial innovation, but Goldman's historical work shows the keynote can generate meaningful EUR/USD movement with the distribution of moves widening considerably AFTER the speech begins, not during the opening minutes. The sideline interviews could matter as much as the formal program, especially with Warsh reluctant to give forward guidance — markets will be listening for Sept-Dec policy clues regardless of the academic theme.
items.angle: Position for a multi-hour vol event, not a single print-and-fade — Goldman's own data says the real signal comes from off-script Q&A, not the prepared remarks.
items.tweetA: Warsh's Jackson Hole keynote topic is literally 'financial innovation' — a decoy. Goldman's own data shows EUR/USD vol keeps widening well past the opening minutes. The trade isn't the speech, it's the hallway interviews afterward.
items.tweetB: Every Jackson Hole, everyone front-runs the first 5 minutes and ignores the tail. Goldman's history says the distribution of FX moves widens AFTER the keynote starts, not during. Fade the instant reaction, position for the drift.

charts.desc: No charts in this note; likely EUR/USD volatility-by-time-since-keynote chart in Goldman's underlying research.

items.title: Goldman's FX desk: the Dollar is becoming the fiscal-dominance release valve
items.idea: Goldman's FX desk argues that if Washington keeps resisting letting long Treasury yields rise enough to attract marginal demand, the pressure migrates into FX instead — not a blanket Dollar-collapse call, since foreign demand for US assets remains intact, but the policy mix of heavy Treasury supply, a steady Fed, and a more activist Treasury is becoming less supportive for the currency. MXN is preferred as steadier carry, CAD improves as trade risk fades, and Asia splits between stronger tech-linked currencies and more vulnerable energy importers. Jackson Hole is the next pressure test.
items.angle: Same underlying mechanism as the Noahpinion Treasury piece below (fiscal dominance, Bessent's bond-market intervention) but seen from the FX plumbing side instead of the yield itself — two angles on one story, worth holding together.
items.tweetA: Goldman's FX desk just said the quiet part: if Bessent won't let long yields rise to clear the market, the pressure has to go somewhere — and it's going into the Dollar. That's fiscal dominance showing up in FX before it fully shows up in bonds.
items.tweetB: Two different desks are describing the same mechanism this week: Treasury intervention buys a day of lower yields, then the pressure resurfaces elsewhere. Goldman says it resurfaces in FX. Watch MXN and CAD as the release valves, not EUR.

items.title: Gold was breaking higher before the news that supposedly caused it
items.idea: Goldman flags gold's rally accelerating as options call-buying turns into its own fuel — a reflexive dynamic where dealer hedging of call flow forces further buying. The key detail: bullion was already breaking higher before whatever catalyst/announcement is being credited actually landed.
items.angle: A gamma-driven melt-up is a different animal from a fundamentals-driven one — it can run further and faster than positioning data implies, and unwind just as violently once dealer hedging flips.
items.tweetA: Gold was breaking higher before the news that supposedly caused the breakout even landed. That's the tell that this leg is options-flow driven, not headline-driven — dealers chasing gamma on call buying, not investors reacting to a catalyst.
items.tweetB: When a rally is a call-buying feedback loop, the question isn't 'why is gold going up' — it's 'when does dealer hedging run out of room.' Worth tracking gold options open interest here more than the next Fed headline. $GLD

charts.desc: No chart in this short note — likely gold price vs. call open-interest chart in Goldman's full research.

items.title: Bessent's bond-buyback intervention bought exactly one day of relief
items.idea: The 30-year Treasury yield jumped 6bps, then after Bessent's surprise announcement of increased long-bond buybacks pushed yields down for exactly one day, it bounced right back — rising over 7bps to as much as 5.27%, right back where it was before the intervention. Noah Smith's own read: the yield rise since early 2026 is 'only a few tenths of a percent,' dwarfed by the sustained 2022-2023 move, so this isn't yet a Cochrane-style bond-vigilante crisis — but he explicitly flags it as the pattern ('gradually, then suddenly') that would precede one.
items.angle: Pair with the Goldman FX item above — if Treasury's main lever only buys one day of relief, the market is already testing whether the government can control the long end, and that test result matters more into Jackson Hole than the yield level itself.
items.tweetA: Bessent's Treasury buyback program bought exactly one day of lower long yields before the 30-year round-tripped back to 5.27%. That's the market telling Treasury its main tool doesn't work at this size. The failed intervention matters more than the yield print.
items.tweetB: Noah Smith's chart says the 2026 Treasury yield rise is 'a few tenths of a percent' — trivial next to 2022-23. He's right on magnitude, but a failed government bond-buying intervention is exactly the 'gradually, then suddenly' pattern Cochrane warned about.

charts.desc: Two embedded charts: global long-term yields showing most of the rise happened 2021-2023 (ex-Japan), and a US-only decade view showing the 2026 move is small versus the 2022-2023 spike. Worth opening.
